{{short description|Tiling puzzle}}
[[File:Eternity_puzzle_board.svg|thumb|An empty Eternity board]]
The '''Eternity puzzle''' is a [[tiling puzzle]] created by [[Christopher Monckton, 3rd Viscount Monckton of Brenchley|Christopher Monckton]] and launched by the [[Ertl Company]] in June 1999. It was marketed as being practically unsolvable, with a £1 million prize on offer for whoever could solve it within four years. The prize was paid out in October 2000 for a winning solution arrived at by two mathematicians from [[Cambridge]].<ref name=scoop>{{citation |title= £1m Eternity jackpot scooped |date= 2000-10-26 |work= [[BBC News]] |url= https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/entertainment/992393.stm }}</ref> A follow-up [[Puzzle contest|prize puzzle]] called [[Eternity II puzzle|Eternity II]] was launched in 2007.<ref name=thescot012407>{{cite web
|url=http://thescotsman.scotsman.com/scotland/Aristocrat-admits-tale-of-lost.3340554.jp
|title=Aristocrat admits tale of lost home was stunt to boost puzzle sales
|work=The Scotsman
|date=2007-01-24
|accessdate=2007-01-24
}}</ref>

== Description ==
The puzzle's scope was to fill a large [[Equiangular polygon|equiangular]] (but not [[Equilateral polygon|equilateral]]) [[dodecagon]] board with 209 puzzle pieces. The board is equipped with a [[Triangular tiling|triangular grid]] made of [[Equilateral triangle|equilateral triangles]]. Its sides alternate in length: six sides coincide with the grid and are 7 triangles (placed edge-to-edge) long, while the other sides are slightly shorter and measure 8 triangles base-to-tip, which equals <math>4\sqrt{3} \approx 6.9</math> edge lengths.

Each puzzle piece is a 12-[[polydrafter]] (dodecadrafter) made of twelve [[30-60-90 triangles]] (that is, a continuous compound of twelve halves of equilateral triangles, restricted to the grid layout). Each piece has an area equal to that of 6 equilateral triangles, and the area of the entire dodecagon is exactly 209 * 6 = 1254 equilateral triangles' (or 2508 [[30-60-90 triangle|drafters]]) worth.<ref name="scoop" /><ref name=":0">{{Cite web|last=Wainwright|first=Mark|date=January 1, 2001|title=Prize specimens|url=https://plus.maths.org/content/prize-specimens|access-date=2020-10-05|website=Plus magazine|language=en}}</ref>

A hint piece was shown placed on every board and solution sheet, although it was not required to be placed there in any solution submission for the prize. Five other hints could be obtained by solving three smaller clue puzzles, which were sold separately.

== Solution ==

As soon as the puzzle was launched, an online community emerged devoted to solving it, centred on a mailing list<ref>{{cite web
|url=http://tech.groups.yahoo.com/group/eternity/messages
|archive-url=https://archive.today/20130105084910/http://tech.groups.yahoo.com/group/eternity/messages
|url-status=dead
|archive-date=January 5, 2013
|title=Eternity mailing list
|accessdate=2011-09-28
}}</ref> on which many ideas and techniques were discussed. It was soon realised that it was trivial to fill the board almost completely, to an "end-game position" where an irregularly-shaped void had to be filled with only a few pieces, at which point the pieces left would be the "wrong shapes" to fill the remaining space. The hope of solving the end-game depended vitally on having pieces that were easy to tile together in a variety of shapes. Computer searches were carried out to find which pieces tiled well or badly, and these data used to alter otherwise-standard [[backtracking search]] programs to use the bad pieces first, in the hope of being left with only good pieces in the hard final part of the search. 

The puzzle was solved on May 15, 2000, before the first deadline, by two [[Cambridge]] mathematicians, Alex Selby and Oliver Riordan.<ref name="archduke061607">{{cite web
|url=http://www.archduke.org/eternity/method/desc.html
|title=Description of (Eternity solver) method
|work=Alex Selby (and Oliver Riordan)
|date=2007-06-16
|accessdate=2007-06-16
}}</ref> Key to their success was the mathematical rigour with which they approached the problem of determining the tileability of individual pieces and of empty regions within the board. These provided measures of the probability that a given piece could help to fill or 'tile' a given region, and the probability that a given region could be tiled by some combination of pieces. In the search for a solution, these probabilities were used to identify which partial tilings, out of a vast number explored by the computer program, were most likely to lead to a solution. A complete solution<ref>{{Cite web|last=Selby|first=Alex|date=|title=[Eternity] Solution|url=http://www.archduke.org/eternity/solution/index.html|access-date=2020-10-05|website=www.archduke.org}}</ref> was obtained within seven months of development with the aid of two domestic PCs.

A second solution<ref>{{Cite web|last=Pegg|first=Ed Jr.|date=|title=The Eternity Puzzle|url=https://www.mathpuzzle.com/eternity.html|access-date=2020-10-05|website=MathPuzzle}}</ref> was found independently by Guenter Stertenbrink and submitted just 6 weeks later, on July 1, 2000.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web|last=Selby|first=Alex|date=|title=Eternity page|url=http://www.archduke.org/eternity/|access-date=2020-10-05|website=www.archduke.org}}</ref> No other solutions have since been published, and the originally intended solution also remains unpublished.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|last=Weisstein|first=Eric W.|title=Eternity|url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/Eternity.html|access-date=2020-10-05|website=mathworld.wolfram.com|language=en}}</ref>

Neither of the known solutions have any of the six hint pieces correctly placed.<ref name=":1" /> According to Alex Selby the puzzle was actually significantly easier to solve without enforcing any fixed hint pieces.<ref name=":0" /> 

== Prize ==
The puzzle's inventor, [[Christopher Monckton, 3rd Viscount Monckton of Brenchley| Christopher Monckton]], put up half the prize money himself, the other half being put up by [[underwriters]] in the London insurance market. According to Eternity's rules, possible solutions to the puzzle would be received by mail on September 21, 2000.  If no correct solutions were opened, the mail for the next year would be kept until September 30, 2001, the process being repeated every year until 2003, after which no entries would be accepted.

Before marketing the puzzle, Monckton had thought that it would take at least three years before anyone could crack the puzzle.<ref name=scoop /> One estimate made at the time stated that the puzzle had 10<sup>500</sup> possible attempts at a solution, and it would take longer than the lifetime of the Universe to calculate all of them even if you had a million computers.<ref>{{citation|author=Duncan Richer|title=The Eternity Puzzle|date=July 1999|url=http://nrich.maths.org/public/viewer.php?obj_id=1354&part=index&refpage=articles.php|publisher=[[NRICH]]}}</ref>

Once solved, Monckton claimed that the earlier-than-expected solution had forced him to sell his 67-room house, [[Crimonmogate]], to pay the prize.<ref name=scoop/><ref name=thescot012407 /> In 2006, he said that the claim had been a [[Public relations|PR]] stunt to boost sales over Christmas, that the house's sale was unrelated to the prize as he was going to sell it anyway.<ref name=thescot012407 />

== Influence ==

The architectural design of the [[Perth Arena]] in [[Perth, Western Australia|Perth]], [[Western Australia]], was heavily influenced by the eternity puzzle; the exterior design is also strongly reflected throughout the main arena, foyers, breakout function rooms and the entrance to the venue.<ref>{{cite web|title=Ashton Raggatt McDougall turn to colour for Perth Arena|url=http://www.architectureanddesign.com.au/article/Ashton-Raggatt-McDougall-turn-to-colour-for-Perth-Arena/515833.aspx|publisher=Architecture & Design|accessdate=18 May 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110117085943/http://architectureanddesign.com.au/article/Ashton-Raggatt-McDougall-turn-to-colour-for-Perth-Arena/515833.aspx|archive-date=17 January 2011|url-status=dead}}</ref>
